blocks.text:
Before Java 5 every container held `Object`. You put a `String` in, you got an `Object` out, and you cast it back and hoped. If somebody had stored an `Integer` in the same list, the program compiled happily and failed at runtime with a `ClassCastException`, possibly far from the line that did the damage. **Generics** move that check to compile time: you tell the compiler "this list holds `String`", and it refuses to compile code that violates the promise and inserts the casts for you.

Generics are also one of the most misunderstood parts of the language, because they were added in a way that kept old bytecode working. The result is a feature that looks like C++ templates but behaves very differently underneath. This chapter teaches the syntax, then the rules that surprise people (wildcards, erasure, arrays), and finally why those rules exist.

### Why generics: the problem and the promise

Here is the pre-generics world, still legal today if you use raw types:

blocks.title: RawDemo.java

blocks.text:
With `List<String>` the line `books.add(42)` is a compile error, and `books.get(0)` needs no cast. Generics give you three things: **type safety** (errors found by the compiler), **no casts** in client code, and **reusable algorithms** (one `max` method works for every comparable type).

### Generic classes, interfaces and methods

A **type parameter** is a placeholder name declared in angle brackets. By convention it is a single capital letter: `T` (type), `E` (element), `K`/`V` (key/value), `R` (result), `N` (number).

blocks.title: Pair.java

blocks.code:
$ java Pair.java
Box[value=Dune] -> Box[value=4]
9
zebra
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- `Box<T>` is a **generic class**: `T` is chosen by whoever writes `Box<String>`. The `<>` on the right of `new Box<>(...)` is the **diamond**; the compiler infers the type argument (Java 7+).
- `map` declares its own `<R>`. A **generic method** has its type parameters before the return type. Callers almost never write them out because the compiler **infers** them from the arguments (`max(List.of(3, 9, 4))` infers `T =` `Integer`). You can force them with `Collections.<String>emptyList()` when inference fails.
- `T extends Comparable<T>` is a **bound**: only types that can compare themselves to their own kind are allowed, which is what lets us call `compareTo`. For several bounds use `&`: `<T extends Number & Comparable<T>>` (a class bound, if any, must come first).
- The same syntax works for interfaces (`interface Repository<T, ID>`) and constructors, and `static` methods can be generic even though a static method cannot use the class's own `T`.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: The word `extends` in a bound means "is a subtype of" and covers interfaces too. There is no `implements` in type bounds. There is also no `T super X` for a type parameter declaration; `super` appears only in wildcards.

### Generics are invariant

Is a `List<Integer>` a `List<Number>`? Intuition says yes, since `Integer` is a `Number`. The compiler says no, and the reason is worth understanding. Suppose it were allowed:

blocks.code:
List<Integer> ints = new ArrayList<>();
List<Number> nums = ints;      // imagine this compiled
nums.add(3.14);                // legal for List<Number>... but ints now holds a Double
Integer i = ints.get(0);       // would blow up
blocks.title: Bad1.java

blocks.code:
$ javac Bad1.java
Bad1.java:5: error: incompatible types: List<Integer> cannot be converted to List<Number>
        List<Number> nums = ints;
                            ^
blocks.title: What javac actually says

blocks.text:
Generic types are **invariant**: `List<Integer>` and `List<Number>` are unrelated types even though `Integer` extends `Number`. Arrays, by contrast, are **covariant** (`Integer[]` is an `Object[]`), which is exactly why `Object[] a = new` `Integer[1]; a[0] = "x";` compiles and throws `ArrayStoreException` at runtime. Generics chose compile-time safety over that convenience.

Invariance is too strict for real code. A method that only sums numbers should accept a `List<Integer>` and a `List<Double>`. That is what wildcards are for.

### Wildcards and PECS

A **wildcard** `?` stands for "some unknown type". It comes in three flavours:

rows: read elements as Object; add only null
list of Number or a subtype (upper bound)
read as Number; cannot add (except null)
list of Integer or a supertype (lower bound)
add Integer; read only as Object

blocks.text: The memory aid is **PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super** (Joshua Bloch). If a structure *produces* values that your code reads, use `? extends T`. If it *consumes* values that your code writes into it, use `? super T`. If you do both, use an exact `T` and no wildcard.

blocks.title: Wild.java

blocks.text: Why can you not add to a `List<? extends Number>`? The compiler only knows "some subtype of Number". It could be a `List<Double>`, so adding an `Integer` would be wrong, and there is no way to name the actual type. javac reports it with a **capture** variable:

blocks.code:
$ javac Bad1.java
Bad1.java:7: error: incompatible types: int cannot be converted to CAP#1
        ro.add(4);
               ^
  where CAP#1 is a fresh type-variable:
    CAP#1 extends Number from capture of ? extends Number
blocks.title: The error for ro.add(4)

blocks.text:
The JDK follows PECS everywhere. `Collections.copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)` and `Comparator<? super T>` in `List.sort` are textbook cases: sorting a `List<Student>` is fine with a `Comparator<Person>`, because anything that can compare any `Person` can compare students.

#### Wildcard capture helper

`List<?>` has a trap: you cannot write `swap(List<?> l)` using `l.set(0, l.get(1))` because the two `?` are different unknowns to the compiler. The standard trick is a private generic helper, which lets the compiler *capture* the wildcard into a named `T`:

Interview angle
blocks.text: What is the difference between `List<?>`, `List<Object>` and the raw `List`? `List<Object>` is a list whose element type is exactly `Object`; you may add anything, but you cannot pass a `List<String>` to it (invariance). `List<?>` is a list of an unknown type; it accepts any parameterisation but you cannot add to it (only null). Raw `List` switches off generic checking entirely and exists only for backward compatibility; it produces unchecked warnings and can corrupt a list at runtime.

### Type erasure

Generics exist only at compile time. After type checking, javac **erases** them: every type parameter is replaced by its bound (or `Object` if unbounded), casts are inserted where needed, and the class file contains no trace of `String` in `List<String>` except in optional signature metadata. This was a deliberate compatibility decision in Java 5, so that old and new code could run together and the JVM did not have to change.

**Erasure at work**
You can see the inserted casts in bytecode. In `Pair.max` above the call `t.compareTo(best)` compiles to an `invokeinterface` on `Comparable`, preceded by `checkcast` instructions:

blocks.code:
$ javap -c -p -cp out Pair | grep "checkcast\|compareTo"
       7: checkcast     #13   // class java/lang/Comparable
      33: checkcast     #13   // class java/lang/Comparable
      39: invokeinterface #29,  2  // InterfaceMethod Comparable.compareTo:(Object)I
      79: checkcast     #55   // class java/lang/String
blocks.title: javap -c -p Pair (trimmed)

blocks.text:
#### Consequences of erasure

These restrictions all follow from "the type argument does not exist at runtime":

- **No primitives as type arguments.** `List<int>` is illegal; use `List<Integer>` (boxing). That has a memory and speed cost, which is why `IntStream` and primitive-specialised classes exist.
- **No** `new T()`**,** `new T[n]`**, or** `T.class`**.** The JVM would not know which class to instantiate. Pass a `Class<T>` or a `Supplier<T>` when you need to create instances.
- **No** `instanceof List<String>`**.** Only the raw class survives. `o instanceof List<?>` is allowed. Pattern matching with `List<String> l` is rejected unless the cast is provably safe (see the javac message below).
- **No static field of type** `T`, and no generic exceptions (`class MyEx<T> extends Exception` is illegal), because a `catch` clause could not tell `MyEx<String>` from `MyEx<Integer>`.
- **Overloads that erase to the same signature clash**: `void f(List<String>)` and `void f(List<Integer>)` cannot coexist.

**javac messages for the forbidden cases**

A type whose runtime representation carries full information is called **reifiable**: primitives, non-generic classes, raw types, `List<?>`, and arrays of those. `List<String>` is **non-reifiable**. Arrays are reified (an `Integer[]` knows it is an `Integer[]` and checks every store), generics are not, and that mismatch is the source of the next two topics.

#### Same class at runtime

blocks.title: Erasure.java

blocks.code:
$ java Erasure.java
true
public int Erasure$Animal.compareTo(Erasure$Animal) bridge=false
public int Erasure$Animal.compareTo(java.lang.Object) bridge=true
size 1
CCE: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang....
CCE from varargs array: class [Ljava.lang.Object; cannot be cast to class [Ljava.lan
[null, null]
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
Three lessons in one run:

1. **Same runtime class.** `ArrayList<String>` and `ArrayList<Integer>` are both just `ArrayList`. That is why `a.getClass() == b.getClass()` is `true`.
2. **Bridge methods.** `Animal implements Comparable<Animal>` and writes `compareTo(Animal)`. After erasure the interface method is `compareTo(Object)`. To keep polymorphism working javac generates a synthetic **bridge** **method** `compareTo(Object)` that casts its argument to `Animal` and calls the real one. Reflection shows both; `bridge=true` marks the generated one. Bridge methods also appear for covariant return types. If you ever see an odd extra method in a stack trace or a `javap` listing, this is it.
3. **Heap pollution and where the exception appears.** A variable of type `List<String>` ended up holding an `Integer`. This is **heap pollution**. The `add(42)` through the raw type only produced a compiler warning; the failure came later at `strings.get(0)`, at a cast the compiler had silently inserted, and the stack trace points at a line that looks perfectly innocent. This is why unchecked warnings should be treated as real bugs, not noise.

### Generic arrays and varargs

`new List<String>[10]` and `new T[10]` are compile errors. If they were allowed, covariance of arrays and erasure would combine to defeat type safety: you could store a `List<Integer>` into what the compiler thinks is a `List<String>[]`, because at runtime the array only checks for `List`. The legal alternatives:

- Use a `List<List<String>>` (almost always the right answer).
- Create `new ArrayList[10]` or `(T[]) new Object[10]` and accept an unchecked cast, keeping the array private (this is what `ArrayList` itself does internally with `Object[]`).
- Use `Array.newInstance(componentClass, n)` when the caller supplies a `Class<T>`.

A **generic varargs** parameter (`T... xs`) is secretly a generic array, so javac warns about "possible heap pollution". In the listing, `bad` returns the varargs array, and `makeArray` calls it from a generic context. At runtime the array is really an `Object[]` (the erasure of `T[]`), so the caller's `String[] arr = ...` cast fails with a `ClassCastException`. `@SafeVarargs` is a promise that you only read the array and never leak it; `List.of`, `Arrays.asList` and `EnumSet.of` make that promise honestly. Leaking the array, as `bad` does, breaks it.

### Raw types and migration

A **raw type** is a generic class used without type arguments (`List`, `Map`). It exists for old code. Using it turns off generic checking for that variable, and mixing raw and parameterised types gives "unchecked" warnings. Do not use raw types in new code. If you must call a legacy API that returns one, convert at the boundary and isolate the suppression:

blocks.title: Legacy.java

blocks.code:
$ java Legacy.java
ADA
LINUS
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text: Keep `@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")` on the smallest scope possible (a single statement or method), with a comment saying why it is safe. Never on a whole class.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: A generic method call can be fine at compile time and still throw `ClassCastException` on a line that has no cast in your source. Whenever a generic return value is used as a concrete type, the compiler inserted a `checkcast`. If the stack trace points at such a line, look for raw types, unchecked casts or `@SuppressWarnings` upstream.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In Spring, `RestTemplate.exchange(..., new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<Order>>() {})` exists purely because of erasure: `List<Order>.class` is not a thing, so the library captures the type argument through an anonymous subclass (its superclass signature is stored in the class file and survives erasure). Jackson has the same idea in `TypeReference`. Knowing erasure explains why these odd-looking helpers are needed.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What is type erasure, and what problems does it cause? The compiler checks generic types, then removes them: type parameters become their bounds (or Object) and casts are inserted. Consequences: no `new T()`, no `T[]`, no `instanceof` `List<String>`, no primitive type arguments, `List<String>` and `List<Integer>` share one runtime class, bridge methods are generated to keep overriding working, and heap pollution is possible through raw types. The upside is full backward compatibility with pre-5 code.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Generics give compile-time type safety and remove casts; the JVM itself only sees erased types.

- Generic types are invariant: `List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`. Use wildcards for flexibility: `? extends` to read, `?` `super` to write (PECS).
- Erasure replaces type parameters by their bounds; that is why there is no `new T()`, no generic arrays, no `instanceof` `List<String>`, and no primitives as type arguments.
- Bridge methods keep overriding working after erasure; heap pollution through raw types fails later at an inserted cast.
- Never use raw types in new code; confine unchecked casts to the smallest annotated scope.

Almost every program keeps groups of things: the books on a shelf, the orders waiting to be shipped, the students in a class. Arrays can hold a group, but they have a fixed size, no built-in search, and no way to say "no duplicates" or "keep these sorted". The **Java Collections Framework** (JCF, in `java.util`, since Java 1.2) is a set of interfaces, implementations and algorithms for groups of objects. Learning it well pays off in every interview and every codebase: choosing the right collection is one of the most common design decisions a Java developer makes.

The framework has a simple split worth memorising before anything else:

- **Interfaces** say what a collection can do: `List`, `Set`, `Queue`, `Deque`, `Map`.
- **Implementations** say how it does it, with different speed and memory trade-offs: `ArrayList`, `LinkedList`, `HashSet`, `TreeSet`, `ArrayDeque`, `PriorityQueue`, `HashMap`, `TreeMap`.
- **Algorithms** are static helpers in `Collections` and `Arrays` (sorting, searching, shuffling).

Program to the interface (`List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();`), so you can swap the implementation without touching callers.

blocks.text: The surprise for beginners: `Map` **does not extend** `Collection`. A collection is a group of single elements; a map is a group of key-value pairs, and operations like `add(E)` make no sense for it. A map exposes three collection **views**: `keySet()`, `values()` and `entrySet()`. We can confirm the hierarchy with reflection:

blocks.title: Iface.java

blocks.code:
$ java Iface.java
2 true false
xy
ArrayList List=true Set=false Queue=false Deque=false Collection=true
LinkedList List=true Set=false Queue=true Deque=true Collection=true
HashSet List=false Set=true Queue=false Deque=false Collection=true
LinkedHashSet List=false Set=true Queue=false Deque=false Collection=true
TreeSet List=false Set=true Queue=false Deque=false Collection=true
ArrayDeque List=false Set=false Queue=true Deque=true Collection=true
PriorityQueue List=false Set=false Queue=true Deque=false Collection=true
HashMap List=false Set=false Queue=false Deque=false Collection=false
TreeMap List=false Set=false Queue=false Deque=false Collection=false

blocks.text: Note that `LinkedList` is both a `List` and a `Deque`, while `ArrayDeque` is a `Deque` only. Here is the family at a glance:

rows: ordered by position, duplicates allowed, index access
holds elements for processing; head and tail operations
blocks.caption: The core interfaces.

blocks.text:
Java 21 added a refinement to this picture: **sequenced collections** (`SequencedCollection`, `SequencedSet`, `SequencedMap`) for types that have a defined first and last element. We cover them at the end of this Part's first half; the diagrams above show them in the hierarchy.

### What every Collection can do

`Collection<E>` defines the operations shared by lists, sets and queues. The ones you use daily:

rows: Number of elements; isEmpty() is clearer than size() == 0.
Uses equals(). Cost depends on the implementation (O(1) HashSet, O(n) ArrayList).
Return boolean: did the collection change? A Set.add of a duplicate returns false.
Bulk operations; retainAll is set intersection, removeAll is set difference.
Java 8. Removes matching elements safely, without an explicit iterator.
Traversal. Every Collection is Iterable, so it works in an enhanced for loop.
Bridge to streams (see the Part on lambdas and streams) and to arrays.
blocks.caption: Core Collection methods.

blocks.text:
Several of these mutators are **optional operations**: an unmodifiable collection (for example `List.of(...)`) implements `add` but throws `UnsupportedOperationException`. This was a design compromise to avoid a separate read-only interface hierarchy. We return to it in the chapter on immutable collections.

### Iteration and Iterator

The enhanced `for` loop is syntactic sugar over an `Iterator`. `for (String b : books)` compiles to roughly `Iterator<String> it = books.iterator(); while (it.hasNext()) { String b = it.next(); ... }`. Any class implementing `Iterable<T>` can be the target of a for-each, including your own:

blocks.title: Shelf.java

blocks.code:
$ java Shelf.java
Dune
Emma
Ulysses
Dune -> 3
Emma -> 0
Ulysses -> 5
{Dune=3, Ulysses=5} keys=[Dune, Ulysses]
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
What to notice: the `Iterator` is a small object with a cursor. It is **single use**: once exhausted, ask the collection for a new one. `Iterator` has three methods (`hasNext`, `next`, optionally `remove`), and `List` adds `ListIterator` with `hasPrevious`, `set` and `add` for bidirectional traversal. The map views are live: `stock.values().removeIf(...)` changed the map itself.

### Fail-fast iterators and ConcurrentModificationException

The most common collections bug in beginner code is changing a list while looping over it. Watch what happens:

blocks.title: Cme.java

blocks.code:
$ java Cme.java
CME: java.util.ConcurrentModificationException
[Dune, Ulysses, Hamlet]
[Dune, Ulysses, Hamlet]
[Dune]
[a, c]
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
Four things happened:

1. The first loop removed "Emma" with `List.remove` while the loop's iterator was active. The next call to `next()` threw `ConcurrentModificationException` (CME). The element *was* removed before the exception (`[Dune, Ulysses,` `Hamlet]`).
2. The explicit `Iterator.remove()` is the supported way to delete during traversal. Here nothing started with "E" any more, so the list is unchanged; run it on a fresh list and it removes correctly.
3. `removeIf` does the same job in one line and is the best choice since Java 8.
4. The last example is the famous silent case: removing the second-to-last element makes `hasNext()` return false, so the loop ends without throwing, and the program carries on with no error. Fail-fast is **best-effort**, not a guarantee.

How it works: `ArrayList` keeps a counter `modCount` that is incremented on every **structural modification** (add, remove, clear; changing an element with `set` does not count). An iterator copies `modCount` when created (`expectedModCount`) and `next()` compares them first. `hasNext()` only checks `cursor != size`, which is why case 4 slips through. The iterator's own `remove()` updates `expectedModCount`, so it stays in sync.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Never rely on a CME to detect a threading bug. The documentation says fail-fast behaviour cannot be guaranteed, particularly under unsynchronised concurrent modification. If several threads share a collection, use a concurrent collection (`ConcurrentHashMap`, `CopyOnWriteArrayList`, covered in the Part on concurrency) or a lock. The CME name is misleading: single-threaded code triggers it all the time.

The opposite design is a **weakly consistent** (or snapshot) iterator. `CopyOnWriteArrayList` iterates over a snapshot and `ConcurrentHashMap` iterators tolerate concurrent changes; neither ever throws a CME.

### equals and hashCode: what collections need from your classes

Collections do not magically know when two of your objects are "the same". They ask the objects:

- `List.contains`, `indexOf`, `remove(Object)` call `equals`.
- Hash-based collections (`HashSet`, `HashMap` keys, `LinkedHashSet`) call `hashCode` first to find a bucket, then `equals` to compare inside it.
- Tree-based collections (`TreeSet`, `TreeMap`) never call `equals`; they use `compareTo` or a `Comparator` (next chapters).

The contract: equal objects must have equal hash codes. Break it and hash collections silently misbehave:

blocks.title: Eq.java

blocks.code:
$ java Eq.java
false
true
true
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
The same two `Isbn` objects are "found" by the `ArrayList` (which uses `equals` only) but not by the `HashSet`: the inherited identity `hashCode` sends the lookup to a different bucket, so `equals` is never even called. A `record` gets a correct `equals` and `hashCode` for free. The full story of buckets is in the HashMap chapter later in this Part.

Two more rules: never use a mutable field in `hashCode` for an object you keep in a hash collection (change it and the object is lost in the wrong bucket), and keep `equals` consistent with `compareTo` when you use sorted collections.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Why does the enhanced for loop throw `ConcurrentModificationException` when you remove an element, and how do you fix it? The list's iterator records the list's modification count when created and checks it on every `next()`. A direct `list.remove` changes the count, so the next `next()` throws. Fix: use `Iterator.remove()`, `removeIf`, collect the items to remove and call `removeAll`, or iterate over a copy. In multi-threaded code use a concurrent collection.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring Data repositories return `List<T>`, `Set<T>` or `Optional<T>`; Hibernate swaps in its own persistent collection classes behind those interfaces. This only works because you coded to the interface. Entities used as `Set` elements or `Map` keys need a careful `equals`/`hashCode` (often based on a business key, not a generated id), which is a classic JPA interview topic.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
The framework separates interfaces (List, Set, Queue, Deque, Map) from implementations; code to the interface.

- `Map` is not a `Collection`; it offers `keySet`, `values` and `entrySet` views that write through to the map.
- Iterators are fail-fast and best-effort: use `Iterator.remove()` or `removeIf` to delete while traversing, never `list.remove` inside for-each.
- Hash collections need a consistent `equals` and `hashCode`; sorted collections need a consistent ordering. Records give you both for free.
- Some mutators are optional operations and throw `UnsupportedOperationException` on unmodifiable collections.

A `List` is an ordered collection that allows duplicates and lets you reach elements by position. It is the collection you will use most. Two implementations dominate the discussion: `ArrayList`, which stores elements in an array, and `LinkedList`, which stores them in chained nodes. Textbooks teach them as equals with opposite strengths; real-world measurement says something much more one-sided. This chapter shows how `ArrayList` actually works, why `LinkedList` is rarely the right answer, and the half-dozen traps (`remove`, `Arrays.asList`, `subList`, `List.of`) that cost beginners hours.

### ArrayList internals

`ArrayList` wraps a plain `Object[] elementData` plus an `int size`. The array length is the **capacity**; `size` is how many slots are in use. `get(i)` is an array read after a bounds check, so it is O(1). `add(e)` writes into the next free slot, O(1) most of the time. When the array is full, `ArrayList` allocates a bigger one (about 1.5 times larger) and copies everything across with `Arrays.copyOf`. This copying is why the growth is called **amortised** O(1): an occasional O(n) copy is spread over many cheap adds.

$ java --add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED Growth.java
new ArrayList(): capacity 0
after add #1: capacity 0 -> 10
after add #11: capacity 10 -> 15
after add #16: capacity 15 -> 22
after add #23: capacity 22 -> 33
after add #34: capacity 33 -> 49
after add #50: capacity 49 -> 73
after add #74: capacity 73 -> 109
new ArrayList(50): capacity 50
copy of 3: capacity 3
after trimToSize: size 10 capacity 10
blocks.title: Run it (JDK 21)

blocks.text:
What the numbers tell you:

- A new `ArrayList` allocates **nothing** until the first add: capacity 0, then 10 on the first `add`. The oft-quoted "default capacity 10" is true, but lazy. Thousands of empty lists cost almost no array memory.
- After that, new capacity = old + old/2 (integer division, `old >> 1`): 10, 15, 22, 33, 49, 73, 109. That is the 1.5x growth.
- `new ArrayList<>(50)` reserves exactly 50, and copying a collection sizes to the collection. If you know roughly how many elements are coming, say so in the constructor (or call `ensureCapacity`) to skip the intermediate copies.
- `trimToSize()` shrinks the array to `size`, useful for a long-lived list that has stopped growing. `clear()` does not shrink the array.

**Inserting or removing in the middle** is O(n): `add(index, e)` and `remove(index)` use `System.arraycopy` to shift every later element by one. It is a fast native block copy, but still proportional to the number of elements moved. `remove` also nulls out the last slot so the removed object can be garbage collected.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.text: `ArrayList` is not thread-safe. Concurrent adds can lose elements or throw `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`. For occasional wrapping use `Collections.synchronizedList`; for read-heavy shared lists see `CopyOnWriteArrayList` below.

### LinkedList: the reality

`LinkedList` is a **doubly linked list**: each element lives in its own `Node` object holding the item and `prev`/`next` references. It implements both `List` and `Deque`. On paper it has O(1) insertion and removal at both ends and O(1) insertion "in the middle" once you hold the position. But finding position `i` means walking from the nearer end, so `get(i)` is O(n).

Textbook claim: "use `LinkedList` when you insert and delete a lot." Here is what the numbers look like for a mixed workload, measured on the build machine (a slow shared sandbox, so only the ratios matter; typical output):

blocks.title: Reality.java

blocks.code:
$ java Reality.java
get(i) loop: ArrayList 43 ms, LinkedList 12416 ms | add(0,x): ArrayList 665 ms, LinkedList 169 ms
get(i) loop: ArrayList 24 ms, LinkedList 5797 ms | add(0,x): ArrayList 600 ms, LinkedList 26 ms
get(i) loop: ArrayList 0 ms, LinkedList 5131 ms | add(0,x): ArrayList 488 ms, LinkedList 5 ms
blocks.title: Typical output (measured on the build machine, varies per run)

blocks.text:
Indexing a `LinkedList` in a loop is catastrophically slow (quadratic overall), and it is the classic way the "obvious" code goes wrong. Inserting at the front is where `LinkedList` shines. But the honest summary is:

- **Default to** `ArrayList`**.** Contiguous arrays are friendly to CPU caches and to the garbage collector; each `LinkedList` node is a separate heap object (on a typical 64-bit HotSpot with compressed references, roughly 24 bytes of node overhead per element on top of the element itself, against 4 bytes per slot in an array).
- Even inserting in the *middle* is usually faster on `ArrayList` for lists of ordinary size, because finding the position in a `LinkedList` costs a pointer walk across scattered memory.
- If you need a queue or a stack (insert and remove at the ends), use `ArrayDeque`, which is faster and lighter than `LinkedList` for that job (see the chapter on queues later in this Part). `LinkedList` remains defensible when you hold a `ListIterator` and do many insertions/removals at the iterator's position, or when you must allow `null` elements in a deque.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: ArrayList vs LinkedList: when would you pick each? ArrayList for almost everything: O(1) random access, compact memory, fast iteration, amortised O(1) append. LinkedList only when you do many insertions/removals at known positions via an iterator or at both ends and never index; even then ArrayDeque is usually better for end operations. Mention that LinkedList.get(i) is O(n) and that node objects cost memory and cache misses; that is the answer that shows you have looked beyond Big-O tables.

### Legacy lists: Vector, Stack, CopyOnWriteArrayList

`Vector` (Java 1.0) is an `ArrayList` whose every method is `synchronized`; `Stack` extends `Vector` and adds `push/pop/peek`. Both predate the Collections Framework. Their per-call locking does not make compound actions atomic ("check then add" still races) and costs speed, and `Stack` inherits list methods that break the stack idea (you can `insertElementAt` in the middle). In new code use `ArrayList`, and `ArrayDeque` as a stack (`push`, `pop`, `peek`). You will still meet `Vector` in old libraries and interview questions.

`CopyOnWriteArrayList` (in `java.util.concurrent`) copies the whole array on every write. Reads and iteration take no lock and see a snapshot, so iteration never throws a CME. It is excellent for lists that are read constantly and changed rarely (a list of event listeners, a configuration list) and terrible for write-heavy use. The concurrency Part covers it properly.

### Remove pitfalls

`List<Integer>` has two methods both named `remove`: `remove(int index)` and `remove(Object o)`. With an `int` argument Java picks the index version, which is almost never what you meant for a list of numbers:

blocks.title: Pitfalls.java

blocks.code:
$ java Pitfalls.java
[10, 30, 1, 2]
[10, 30, 2]
[Z, b, c] [Z, b, c]
asList add: java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException
1
List.of add: java.lang.UnsupportedOperationException
List.of null: NPE
List.of contains(null): NPE
[0, 1, 99, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] [99, 3, 4]
[0, 1, 5, 6, 7]
sub after parent change: CME
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
Go through the output slowly; each block is an interview favourite.

#### remove(int) versus remove(Object)

`nums.remove(1)` removed the element at index 1 (the value 20), not the value 1. To remove by value pass an object: `nums.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))`.

#### Arrays.asList is a fixed-size view

`Arrays.asList(arr)` does not copy. It returns a list **backed by the array**: `set` writes through to the array (`[Z, b, c]` in both), the size cannot change (`add` and `remove` throw `UnsupportedOperationException`). With a primitive array `Arrays.asList(prim)` gives a `List<int[]>` containing one element, because `T...` cannot be `int`. To get a normal mutable list write `new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(arr))` (or `List.of(arr)` for an immutable copy).

#### List.of is immutable and null-hostile

`List.of(...)` (Java 9) returns an **immutable** list. Mutators throw `UnsupportedOperationException`, nulls are rejected in the factory (`NullPointerException`), and even `contains(null)` throws. Compare that with the *unmodifiable view* from `Collections.unmodifiableList`, which only blocks changes through the view. The next chapters in this Part separate those ideas properly.

#### subList is a window, not a copy

`base.subList(2, 5)` is a **view** of the parent over indices 2 to 4. Writes and `clear()` on the view change the parent (the 99 appeared in `base`; `sub.clear()` deleted three elements from it). It is the idiomatic way to delete a range: `list.subList(from, to).clear()`. But if the parent is *structurally* modified directly after the view was created, any use of the view throws a `ConcurrentModificationException`. Treat a `subList` as short-lived; if you need to keep it, copy it: `new ArrayList<>(base.subList(2, 5))`.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: Do not hold on to a `subList` returned from a long-lived list. It keeps the whole parent alive in memory, and any later structural change to the parent invalidates it.

### Everyday list API worth knowing

- `list.sort(comparator)` sorts in place (it delegates to `Arrays.sort` on the backing array, which is a stable merge sort variant; see the chapter on sorting).
- `list.replaceAll(UnaryOperator)` transforms every element in place; `list.removeIf(Predicate)` removes matches in one pass (for `ArrayList` this is a single compaction, O(n), instead of the O(n squared) of repeated `remove`).
- `list.indexOf`, `lastIndexOf`, `contains` use `equals`; `list.equals(other)` is true for any two lists with equal elements in the same order, regardless of implementation.
- `listIterator()` allows moving backwards and `add`/`set` at the cursor.
- `list.toArray(new String[0])` converts to a typed array; the zero-length array is a type token and is the recommended form.
- `Collections.nCopies`, `Collections.emptyList()` and `List.copyOf` build special-purpose immutable lists.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: In Spring services the overwhelmingly common choice is `ArrayList`: query results, JSON arrays deserialised by Jackson and stream `collect(Collectors.toList())` results are all array-backed. The practical rules that matter at work are: return an empty list rather than `null`, do not expose your internal mutable list from a getter (return `List.copyOf(items)` or an unmodifiable view), and never mutate a list you received from a caller, since it might be an immutable `List.of`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
`ArrayList` is an array with lazy first allocation (capacity 10) and about 1.5x growth; `get` is O(1), middle insert/remove is O(n).

- Default to `ArrayList`; `LinkedList.get(i)` is O(n) and its nodes cost memory and cache misses. Use `ArrayDeque` for stacks and queues.
- `remove(int)` versus `remove(Object)` is a classic trap for `List<Integer>`.
- `Arrays.asList` is a fixed-size write-through view of the array; `List.of` is immutable and rejects null; `subList` is a live window onto its parent.
- `Vector` and `Stack` are legacy; `CopyOnWriteArrayList` suits read-mostly shared lists.

A **set** is a collection with one promise: no duplicates. You reach for a set when the question is "have I seen this before?", "which items are in both groups?" or "give me the distinct values". A `List` can answer those questions, but slowly: `list.contains(x)` walks the whole list, so checking a million items against a million-item list is a trillion comparisons. A well-chosen set answers `contains` in constant or logarithmic time.

The `java.util.Set` interface adds almost nothing to `Collection`. It tightens the contract (`add` returns `false` and does nothing if an equal element is already present) and defines what "equal" and "hash" mean for whole sets. The interesting part is the three main implementations, because they differ in ordering and speed. Learn them as a trio.

### HashSet: a HashMap in disguise

`HashSet` does not contain its own hashing logic. Open the JDK source and you will find one field: a `HashMap<E, Object>` called `map`, plus a static dummy value shared by every entry.

blocks.title: HashSetInternals.java (simplified from the JDK source)

blocks.text:
That is the whole idea. The element is the map key; the value is a dummy. `add` returns `true` exactly when `put` found no previous value for the key. Everything you learn in the next chapter about `HashMap` (buckets, hash spreading, resizing, treeification, the cost of a bad `hashCode`) is therefore also true for `HashSet`. `LinkedHashSet` is built the same way on top of `LinkedHashMap`, and `TreeSet` on top of `TreeMap`.

Two consequences matter in practice. First, an element's identity inside a hash set is decided by `hashCode()` and `equals()`, never by `==`. Two distinct `Point` objects with equal fields are the same element if the class overrides both methods (a `record` does so for you). Second, iteration order is whatever the table happens to look like.

blocks.title: SetsDemo.java (part 1: the three orders)

blocks.code:
$ java SetsDemo.java
HashSet:       [banana, apple, pear, kiwi, fig]
LinkedHashSet: [pear, apple, fig, kiwi, banana]
TreeSet:       [apple, banana, fig, kiwi, pear]
add duplicate: false
blocks.title: Run it (the HashSet line is typical; do not depend on it)

blocks.text: The `HashSet` order looks random but is not: it is the order of the buckets in the table, and a bucket is picked from the string's hash code. Because `String.hashCode()` is specified, the same strings in the same-sized table give the same order on every run of the same JDK. Still, a different table size, a different JDK version or a different insertion history can change it. Treat it as unordered. (Sets created with `Set.of(...)` go further: their iteration order is deliberately randomised per JVM start, to stop programs from depending on it.)

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: Constructing a set from a collection is the idiom for removing duplicates: `new HashSet<>(list)` loses order, `new` `LinkedHashSet<>(list)` removes duplicates but keeps first-seen order, `new TreeSet<>(list)` removes duplicates and sorts. Pick by the order you want afterwards.

### LinkedHashSet: predictable order for a small price

`LinkedHashSet` is a `HashSet` whose entries are additionally threaded on a doubly linked list. The hash table still does lookups; the linked list only remembers insertion order, so iteration walks the list instead of scanning empty buckets. The costs are two extra references per entry (about 8 bytes with compressed pointers) and slightly slower inserts. Re-inserting an element that is already present does not move it. Use it whenever a user will see the output, in tests where you compare printed results, and for "distinct but keep order" jobs.

From Java 21 it is a `SequencedSet`, so it has `getFirst()`, `getLast()`, `removeFirst()` and `reversed()`; the sequenced collections are covered in the chapter on immutable and sequenced collections.

### TreeSet and NavigableSet: sorted, with range queries

`TreeSet` keeps its elements sorted using a red-black tree (a self-balancing binary search tree; the chapter on other maps explains the shape). Because it is ordered, it can answer questions a hash set cannot: what is the smallest element at least 25? Which elements fall between 20 and 40? These live in the `NavigableSet` interface (which extends `SortedSet`).

headSet(30)=[10, 20] tailSet(30)=[30, 40, 50]

Note
blocks.text: `headSet`, `tailSet`, `subSet` and `descendingSet` return live **views** of the original tree, not copies. Adding to the original shows up in the view, and adding an out-of-range element to the view throws `IllegalArgumentException`. Wrap in `new` `TreeSet<>(view)` if you want a snapshot.

#### Equality in a TreeSet is decided by compareTo, not equals

`TreeSet` never calls `equals` or `hashCode`. Two elements are "the same" when the comparison returns 0. That is usually what you want, but it surprises people whose comparator looks at only one field.

blocks.title: TreeSetCompare.java

blocks.code:
$ java TreeSetCompare.java
case-insensitive: [Java]
by length: [cat, bird]
not Comparable: ClassCastException
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
The second line is the classic bug: `cat` and `dog` have length 3, so the comparator says they are equal and `dog` is dropped. If your comparator orders by one field, add tie-breakers with `thenComparing` until it only returns 0 for elements you truly consider equal. The third case shows that a `TreeSet` of non-`Comparable` elements fails on the very first `add`, not later. Two more `TreeSet` rules: it rejects `null` (natural ordering cannot compare it), and it is not thread-safe (`ConcurrentSkipListSet` is the sorted concurrent alternative).

### EnumSet: the fastest set you will ever use

When the elements are values of one enum, use `EnumSet`. It is abstract; you create instances through factories such as `EnumSet.of(...)`, `noneOf(Class)`, `allOf(Class)`, `range(a, b)`, `complementOf(set)` and `copyOf(collection)`. Internally an enum set of up to 64 constants is a single `long` used as a bit mask (bit number = the constant's `ordinal()`), larger enums use a `long[]`. `add`, `contains` and `remove` are a shift and a mask; `containsAll`, `retainAll` and `addAll` are one bitwise instruction per word. Iteration is in declaration order of the constants.

blocks.title: EnumSetDemo.java

blocks.code:
$ java EnumSetDemo.java
[SAT, SUN] [MON, TUE, WED, THU, FRI]
range = [TUE, WED, THU]
allOf size = 7
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
Use an `EnumSet<Permission>` instead of an `int` full of flag bits: you get the same speed with type safety and readable output.

### Set algebra with bulk operations

The bulk methods of `Collection` are exactly the mathematical set operations. The trick is that they modify the receiver, so copy first when you need the originals again.

blocks.title: SetAlgebra.java

blocks.code:
$ java SetAlgebra.java
union        = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7]
intersection = [4, 5]
a minus b    = [1, 2, 3]
symmetric    = [1, 2, 3, 6, 7]
a contains all of intersection: true
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
(The helpers copy into a `TreeSet` only so the printed order is stable; use a `HashSet` copy when you do not care.) A performance trap hides in `removeAll`: if the argument is a `List`, each element of the receiver is looked up with `List.contains`, which is O(n). Pass a set as the argument.

### The mutating-element bug

A hash set stores each element in the bucket chosen by its hash code at the time of insertion. If the element changes in a way that alters `hashCode()` while it sits in the set, the set still looks for it in the old bucket and never finds it again. The object is still there, still reachable by iteration, and impossible to look up or remove.

blocks.title: MutationBug.java

blocks.code:
$ java MutationBug.java
contains(t)       = false
size              = 1
iteration         = [jvm]
contains("java")  = false
remove(t)         = false
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
Neither `contains(t)` nor `contains(new Tag("java"))` succeeds: the first looks in the bucket for "jvm" (empty), the second finds the bucket for "java" but the stored object's `equals` no longer matches. The element is leaked until the set is discarded. The same applies to keys of a `HashMap` and to elements of a `TreeSet` whose ordering fields change (the tree is simply mis-ordered).

The rule: **elements of sets and keys of maps must be immutable, or at least their** `equals`**/**`hashCode`**/ordering** **fields must never change while they are in the collection.** Prefer `String`, boxed numbers, enums, `record`s of immutable fields and `java.time` values.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: `Set.of(...)` and `Map.of(...)` reject `null` and also throw `NullPointerException` from `contains(null)`; `HashSet` and `LinkedHashSet` accept one `null`; `TreeSet` accepts none. `Set.of("a", "a")` throws `IllegalArgumentException` for the duplicate. Know which factory you are holding when null is possible.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How does a HashSet guarantee uniqueness, and what happens if you put objects that do not override equals and hashCode? It delegates to a `HashMap`: the element is the key, so `add` computes the hash, finds the bucket and uses `equals` to look for an existing equal key. Without overrides, `Object`'s identity-based versions are used, so two objects with equal fields are treated as different elements and "duplicates" appear. With `hashCode` overridden but `equals` not (or vice versa) the contract is broken and lookups become unreliable.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: When would you choose TreeSet over HashSet? When you need sorted iteration or range/neighbour queries (`floor`, `ceiling`, `subSet`) and can pay O(log n) per operation. If you only test membership, `HashSet` is faster. If the elements are enum constants, use `EnumSet`.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A `HashSet` is a `HashMap` whose values are a dummy; uniqueness comes from `hashCode` and `equals`, so both must be consistent and based on immutable data.
- `LinkedHashSet` keeps insertion order for a small memory cost; `TreeSet` keeps sorted order and offers `NavigableSet` range queries in O(log n), with equality decided by the comparator.
- `EnumSet` is a bit mask: use it for sets of enum constants. Copy before using `addAll`/`retainAll`/`removeAll` if you need the original.
- Mutating an element after insertion makes it unreachable in hash sets and corrupts tree order; keep elements immutable.

sections.title: Other maps: LinkedHashMap, TreeMap and the specialists

blocks.text:
### specialists

`HashMap` is the default, but the `Map` interface has a family of implementations that each trade something for something else. Choosing the right one often replaces twenty lines of hand-written code with a constructor call. This chapter covers the ones you will meet in real code and in interviews, in order of how often you need them.

rows: legacy; do not use in new code
blocks.caption: The Map family at a glance.

blocks.text:
### LinkedHashMap: order and the LRU cache

`LinkedHashMap` extends `HashMap` and additionally threads every entry onto a doubly linked list (each node gets `before` and `after` references). Lookups use the hash table as usual; iteration follows the list. By default the list is in **insertion** **order**. A re-`put` of an existing key does not move it.

The second mode is **access order**. Construct it with the three-argument constructor `new` `LinkedHashMap<>(initialCapacity, loadFactor, true)` and every `get`, `put` or `compute` on a key moves its entry to the end of the list, so the first entry is always the least recently used. Combine that with the protected hook `removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry)`, which `put` calls after inserting; return `true` and the map deletes the eldest entry. That is a complete LRU (least-recently-used) cache in a dozen lines.

blocks.code:
$ java LruCache.java
keys, eldest first: [c, a, d]
contains b? false
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text: After the `get("a")` the order is `b, c, a`; inserting `d` makes the size 4 which exceeds the capacity, so `b` (the eldest) goes. The result is `c, a, d`.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: This LRU cache is not thread-safe, and in access-order mode even `get` modifies the list, so two concurrent readers can corrupt it. Wrap it with `Collections.synchronizedMap` or use a purpose-built cache library (Caffeine is the standard choice in Spring applications). The last chapter of this Part builds an LRU from scratch with a hash map plus your own linked list.

From Java 21, `LinkedHashMap` is a `SequencedMap`: it has `firstEntry()`, `lastEntry()`, `putFirst`, `putLast`, `pollFirstEntry()` and `reversed()`. For example `putFirst("z", 0)` on a map holding a, b, c gives `{z=0, a=1, b=2,` `c=3}`, and `reversed()` shows the entries last-to-first as a view.

### TreeMap: the sorted map

`TreeMap` keeps its entries sorted by key, using a **red-black tree**. Sorted order is the whole point: it supports everything a sorted structure can do, and every basic operation (`put`, `get`, `remove`, `containsKey`) costs O(log n) because the tree is balanced.

#### What a red-black tree is

A binary search tree stores smaller keys in the left subtree and larger keys in the right. Without care, inserting already-sorted keys (1, 2, 3, ...) builds a lopsided chain with O(n) lookups. A red-black tree is a binary search tree whose nodes are coloured red or black, with rules that keep it approximately balanced:

1. The root is black.
2. A red node has only black children (no two reds in a row).
3. Every path from a node down to its empty leaves passes through the same number of black nodes.

Rule 3 and rule 2 together mean that the longest root-to-leaf path is at most twice the shortest, so the height stays at most about 2 log2(n). When an insertion or removal breaks a rule, the tree repairs itself with recolourings and **rotations**, local rearrangements that change the shape but keep the left-smaller-right-larger order. You will not be asked to code deletion, but you should be able to state the rules and the O(log n) guarantee. Each `TreeMap` entry also stores a `left`, a `right`, a `parent` and a colour flag, so it is heavier than a `HashMap` node.

#### NavigableMap in action

`TreeMap` implements `NavigableMap`, the map twin of `NavigableSet`: `firstKey`, `lastKey`, `floorKey/Entry`, `ceilingKey/Entry`, `lowerKey`, `higherKey`, `pollFirstEntry`, `headMap`, `tailMap`, `subMap` and `descendingMap`. The first three examples below are tasks that are awkward to solve any other way.

ceilingKey(61)     = 70
descending keys    = [90, 80, 70, 60, 0]
firstKey           = 0

The `floorEntry` trick (a lookup table with ranges, like tax brackets, shipping rates or the highest bid below a price) is the most useful idea here: with a `HashMap` you would loop over all thresholds.

Like `TreeSet`, a `TreeMap` treats two keys as equal when `compareTo` (or your `Comparator`) returns 0, never consulting `equals`. A comparator that is inconsistent with `equals` makes the map violate the general `Map` contract, while still being internally consistent.

### EnumMap

An `EnumMap<K extends Enum<K>, V>` stores its values in a plain array indexed by the key's `ordinal()`. `get` and `put` are an array access: no hashing, no collisions, and the smallest footprint of any map. Iteration is in enum declaration order. Use it whenever the key is an enum.

blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
### IdentityHashMap: reference equality

`IdentityHashMap` compares keys with `==` and hashes with `System.identityHashCode` instead of `equals`/`hashCode`. It deliberately violates the `Map` contract. Two keys that are `equals` but distinct objects are two entries. You almost never want this in business code. It exists for algorithms that must track *objects* rather than values: a deep copy or serializer that records "I have already visited this exact node" to survive cycles, or a proxy and instrumentation framework.

$ java IdentityDemo.java

HashMap size         = 1
blocks.title: Run it

blocks.text:
### WeakHashMap: entries that disappear

A `WeakHashMap` holds its **keys** through weak references. When a key is no longer strongly reachable from anywhere else, the garbage collector may clear it, and the map silently drops the entry afterwards. It suits caches of metadata keyed by objects whose lifetime you do not control ("extra data about this object, which should vanish when the object does"). Weak, soft and phantom references are explained in the memory chapters of the JVM part.

blocks.code:
$ java WeakDemo.java
before gc: size = 2
after gc:  size = 1
true
blocks.title: Run it (the result depends on the garbage collector acting; this is typical)
Gotcha
blocks.text: The *value* is held strongly. If a value refers back to its own key (directly or through a chain), the key never becomes weakly reachable and the entry never goes away. Also, never use `String` literals or small cached boxed values as keys of a `WeakHashMap`: they are always strongly reachable, so the entries never disappear.

### ConcurrentHashMap: the thread-safe map

When several threads share a map, `HashMap` can lose updates, return stale data or corrupt itself. The correct default is `java.util.concurrent.ConcurrentHashMap`. The full story belongs to the concurrency part; here is what you should know now.

- **Not one big lock.** (The Java 7 version used segments, the Java 8 rewrite does not.) Reads are lock-free. An insert into an **empty bucket** uses a compare-and-set (CAS). Only when the bucket already has nodes does the writer synchronise on that bucket's first node, so two threads writing to different buckets proceed in parallel. Its bins use the same linked-list-then-tree strategy as `HashMap`.
- **Atomic compound operations.** `putIfAbsent`, `computeIfAbsent`, `compute`, `merge` and `replace(k, old, new)` run atomically for that key. `if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v)` is a race even on a concurrent map; `putIfAbsent` is not.
- **No nulls.** Neither null keys nor null values: in a shared map, `get(k) == null` would be ambiguous (absent or mapped to null), and the caller cannot call `containsKey` atomically afterwards.
- **Weakly consistent iterators.** They never throw `ConcurrentModificationException`; they reflect the map at some point at or after the creation of the iterator, and may or may not show later changes.
- `size()` **is an estimate under concurrent change** (it is summed from striped counters, like `LongAdder`). `mappingCount()` returns a `long`.

Do not "fix" the unsafe counter by wrapping each step in your own check-then-act code; use the atomic methods. When you need a sorted concurrent map, use `ConcurrentSkipListMap`.

### Hashtable and Collections.synchronizedMap

`Hashtable` is a Java 1.0 class: every method is `synchronized` on the whole table (one lock for everything), it rejects null keys and values, and it exposes the pre-collections `Enumeration` API. It is kept only for compatibility. Its `Properties` subclass is still common for configuration (see the chapter on properties). In new code use `ConcurrentHashMap` for sharing, or `HashMap` when single-threaded.

`Collections.synchronizedMap(map)` wraps any map with a single mutex. It is safe for individual calls but you must still hold the lock yourself when iterating over its views, and compound operations are not atomic. Prefer `ConcurrentHashMap`.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: How would you implement an LRU cache in Java? Extend `LinkedHashMap` with access order enabled (`super(cap, 0.75f,` `true)`) and override `removeEldestEntry` to return `size() > capacity`. It is O(1) per operation. For a concurrent cache wrap it in a synchronised wrapper or use Caffeine. If the interviewer wants it "from scratch", combine a `HashMap` from key to node with a doubly linked list; the last chapter of this Part shows that version.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: HashMap vs ConcurrentHashMap vs Hashtable? `HashMap`: no synchronisation, one null key, fastest single-threaded. `Hashtable`: legacy, every method locked, no nulls. `ConcurrentHashMap`: scalable thread-safe map with CAS and per-bucket locking, atomic `merge`/`compute`, no nulls, weakly consistent iterators.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: When would you use TreeMap instead of HashMap? When you need keys in sorted order or nearest-key queries (floor, ceiling, subMap), accepting O(log n) instead of O(1) and the extra memory per entry.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- `LinkedHashMap` adds a linked list to `HashMap`: insertion order by default, access order plus `removeEldestEntry` gives an LRU cache.
- `TreeMap` is a red-black tree: sorted keys, O(log n) operations and `NavigableMap` queries (`floor`, `ceiling`, `headMap`, `subMap`); equality is by comparator.
- Use `EnumMap` for enum keys, `IdentityHashMap` for reference semantics, `WeakHashMap` for entries tied to key lifetime.
- For shared maps use `ConcurrentHashMap` with its atomic `merge`/`compute`/`putIfAbsent`; `Hashtable` is legacy.

`HashMap` is the most used class in the Java standard library after `String` and `ArrayList`, and the most asked-about in interviews. Almost every backend program uses one: caches, indexes by id, counters, grouping. Using it is easy. Knowing why `get` is "O(1)", when it stops being O(1), and which mistakes make it silently wrong is what separates a Java user from a Java engineer. This chapter opens the class up, based on the OpenJDK implementation (the structure has been stable since Java 8, and I verified the numbers below by running experiments on JDK 21).

### The problem and the core idea

You want to find a value by key without scanning everything. An array gives you instant access by an integer index, so the idea is: turn the key into an integer, and use that integer to pick a slot in an array. The array is called the **table**; each slot is a **bucket**. The conversion function is `hashCode()`.

Two different keys can map to the same bucket (a **collision**, unavoidable: there are far more possible keys than slots). So a bucket holds not one entry but a small collection of entries, and a lookup is: compute the bucket, then search the few entries inside it using `equals`. If the buckets stay short, the lookup costs a constant number of steps regardless of how many entries the map holds. All the engineering in `HashMap` is about keeping buckets short.

blocks.text:
### From key to bucket: hash spreading and the index

There are two steps, and both are worth knowing exactly.

**Step 1, the spread.** `HashMap` takes the key's `hashCode()` and mixes the high 16 bits into the low 16 bits:

blocks.title: Spread.java (from the JDK source, HashMap.hash)

blocks.text:
A `null` key therefore hashes to 0 and lives in bucket 0 (which is why `HashMap` allows one `null` key). The spread exists because of step 2.

**Step 2, the index.** The table length is always a power of two, so instead of the slow `hash % length` the map computes `(length - 1) & hash`. With length 16 the mask is binary `1111`, so only the lowest 4 bits of the hash choose the bucket. Without the spread, any two hash codes that differ only in their upper bits would always collide in small tables. A concrete case: the integers 65536, 131072 and 196608 differ only in bits 16 and above; in a 16-slot table all three would land in bucket 0. After `h ^ (h >>> 16)` they land in buckets 1, 2 and 3. The spread is a cheap way (one shift, one XOR) to let every bit of the hash influence the index.

Power-of-two sizing also gives the resize a very nice property, which we reach below.

blocks.text:
Read the output carefully, it explains a lot.

- `Aa` and `BB` have the same `hashCode` (2112). This is a famous coincidence of Java's string hash, not a bug; it is a handy source of deliberate collisions for experiments.
- A new `HashMap` has **no table at all** (`table=null`). The table is allocated lazily, on the first `put`, with the default capacity 16.
- The **threshold** is `capacity × load factor`: 16 × 0.75 = 12. When the entry count exceeds it, the table doubles.

### Buckets, collisions and the node

Each bucket starts as `null`. The first entry stored in a bucket is a `HashMap.Node`, which holds exactly four fields: the cached `hash`, the `key`, the `value` and a `next` reference. With compressed pointers (the default on 64-bit JVMs for heaps under about 32 GB) that is a 12-byte object header plus four 4-byte fields: 28 bytes, padded to 32. That per-entry cost is one reason a `HashMap<Integer,Integer>` is much heavier than the numbers it stores (see the chapter on choosing data structures).

`put(key, value)` does the following.

1. If the table is `null`, allocate it (resize to the default 16).
2. Compute `i = (n - 1) & hash(key)`. If bucket `i` is empty, put a new node there. Done.
3. Otherwise walk the bucket. For each node compare the stored hash first, then the key: `node.hash == hash &&` `(node.key == key || key.equals(node.key))`. Comparing the cached hash first is a cheap filter that avoids most `equals` calls.
4. If an equal key is found, replace its value (and return the old value). Otherwise append a new node at the **tail** of the chain.
5. If the number of entries now exceeds the threshold, resize.

`get` is steps 2 and 3 only. Notice what this means for you: `get` calls your key's `hashCode()` once and `equals()` on the keys in one bucket. If `hashCode` is slow or `equals` is wrong, `HashMap` inherits the problem.

### Resizing and rehashing

When `size > threshold` the table doubles (16, 32, 64, ...) and the threshold doubles with it. Every entry must be moved, because its index depends on the table length. Here the power-of-two choice pays off. Going from length 16 to 32 adds one more bit to the mask. For each entry that bit of its hash is either 0 or 1, so an entry in old bucket `j` goes to either new bucket `j` or new bucket `j + 16`, nothing else. The JDK splits every bucket into a "low" list and a "high" list in a single pass, preserving the relative order, without recomputing any hash and without reallocating nodes. That is why the resize loop is simple and why entries from one bucket never mix with others.

Resizing is still O(n) work and allocates a new array, so it is the main source of latency spikes when a map grows. If you know roughly how many entries you will add, size the map up front. Beware the trap in the experiment above: `new` `HashMap<>(100)` does **not** hold 100 entries without resizing. The constructor rounds 100 up to the next power of two, 128, and the threshold is only 96. Since Java 19 there is a factory that does the arithmetic for you: `HashMap.newHashMap(100)` computes `ceil(100 / 0.75)`, then rounds up to 256 here, and guarantees no resize for 100 entries. On older JDKs write `new HashMap<>((int) (n / 0.75f) + 1)`.

#### The load factor

The default load factor of 0.75 is a compromise stated in the Javadoc: it balances time and space cost. A lower value (say 0.5) means shorter buckets and faster lookups but a table twice as big; a higher value (say 1.0 or more) saves memory but buckets get longer. With a decent hash function and load factor 0.75 the average bucket holds well under one entry, and chains of 8 or more are astronomically unlikely by chance (the JDK source comment quotes a Poisson distribution with parameter 0.5, giving a chance of about 6 in 100 million for 8 entries). In practice you leave the load factor alone. Tuning it is almost never the right fix.

### Treeification: Java 8's defence against bad hashes

Before Java 8, a bucket was always a linked list. Lookup in a long chain is O(n), and a bad `hashCode` (or a deliberate attack: crafting thousands of strings with equal hashes to hit a web server's parameter map) could turn a map into a slow linked list. Java 8 added the **tree bin**: when a bucket grows long, its linked list is converted into a red-black tree (the same balanced tree that `TreeMap` uses), so a single worst-case bucket costs O(log n) instead of O(n).

blocks.text:
There is a subtlety that most explanations get wrong. Treeification is attempted when a bucket that already holds 8 nodes receives a 9th (the check in `putVal` is on the count of nodes traversed). And then `treeifyBin` first looks at the table length: if the table has fewer than 64 buckets, it **resizes instead of treeifying**, on the theory that a small table with a long chain simply needs more buckets. Only when the table is at least 64 does the bin become a tree.

You can watch this happen. The next program uses keys whose `hashCode` is the constant 42, so every key goes into the same bucket, and peeks at the table with reflection.

blocks.title: BadHash.java

after 10 keys: table=64, the used bin holds a Node
after 11 keys: table=64, the used bin holds a TreeNode
after 12 keys: table=64, the used bin holds a TreeNode
round 0: non-Comparable 21528 ms | Comparable  815 ms | good  41 ms

blocks.title: Run it (the timings are typical on the build machine; this program takes about a minute and a half)

blocks.text:
What to notice:

- The 9th key into the same bucket did not build a tree; it **doubled the table** from 16 to 32. So did the 10th (to 64). Only the 11th key finally found a table of length 64 and converted the bin into a `TreeNode`.
- Inserting 20,000 keys with a constant hash and no ordering took between 14 and 22 **seconds**; the good keys took milliseconds. A single bad `hashCode` is the difference between a fast service and an outage.
- The third column is the surprise: the same constant hash, but the key class implements `Comparable`, and 20,000 inserts take well under a second. A tree bin orders nodes by hash first and, when hashes are equal, by `compareTo` (if the keys share a class and are `Comparable`). Then it can binary-search, O(log n). If the keys are not `Comparable`, the tree cannot order the colliding nodes; a lookup has to search both subtrees, and the tree degrades to O(n) with a worse constant than the plain list. Treeification is a safety net with a hole: **make keys** `Comparable` **when you** **cannot guarantee a good hash**, and fix the hash regardless.

When removals or a resize shrink a tree bin to 6 nodes or fewer, it is converted back into a plain linked list (the "untreeify" threshold of 6; the gap between 8 and 6 stops a bin from flipping back and forth at the boundary).

### Writing a good hashCode

The `HashMap` contract rests on one rule from `Object`: **equal objects must have equal hash codes.** The reverse need not hold, but the closer hashes of unequal objects are to uniformly distributed, the better. Practical guidance:

- Override `equals` and `hashCode` together, using the same fields.
- Use `Objects.hash(a, b, c)` or, for new code, a `record`, which generates both from all components. `Objects.hash` boxes primitives and allocates an array, so in a very hot path write the arithmetic by hand: `31 * a + b`.
- Never use mutable fields, and never use fields that differ between equal objects (e.g. a timestamp).
- Remember the standard hash codes: `Integer` is its value; `Long` is `(int)(v ^ (v >>> 32))`; `String` is `s[0]*31^(n-1)` `+ ... + s[n-1]` (cached in the string after the first call); `List.hashCode` combines elements the same way as `Objects.hash`. For example `Objects.hash(1, 2, 3)` and `List.of(1, 2, 3).hashCode()` are both 30817.

### The map API that every engineer should use

Older Java code does `if (map.containsKey(k)) { map.put(k, map.get(k) + 1); } else { map.put(k, 1); }`. That hashes the key three times and is not atomic in a concurrent map. Java 8 added single-call methods that read better and do the right thing.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Do not mutate the map from inside `computeIfAbsent`, `compute` or `merge` (for example, a recursive memoised Fibonacci calling `computeIfAbsent` from within its own mapping function). `HashMap` detects it and throws `ConcurrentModificationException` since Java 9.

### Iteration order and fail-fast iterators

Iterating a `HashMap` visits buckets from index 0 to the end, and each chain from head to tail. The order depends on key hashes and the table length, so it can change when the map resizes. Look at integer keys inserted as 33, 17, 1, 49, 16, 2 into a map with 16 buckets: 16 goes to bucket 0; 33, 17, 1 and 49 all share bucket 1 (each is 1 modulo 16) and stay in insertion order within it; 2 goes to bucket 2. The key set prints `[16, 33, 17, 1, 49, 2]`, which is neither insertion nor sorted order. If your program prints a `HashMap` and a test compares the text, you have a flaky test. Use `LinkedHashMap` or `TreeMap` when order matters.

Iterators of `HashMap` are **fail-fast**: the map keeps a `modCount` that every structural change (add or remove an entry, not replacing a value) increments. The iterator remembers the count when it was created and throws `ConcurrentModificationException` on the next step if it changed. This is a best-effort bug detector, not a thread-safety mechanism. To remove entries while iterating use `iterator.remove()` or the bulk forms `map.entrySet().removeIf(...)` and `map.values().removeIf(...)`.

### The key-mutation bug, again, for maps

The earlier chapter on sets showed that mutating an element makes it unfindable. For maps it is the same with keys, and it is a common source of "the data is in the map but `get` returns `null`" bugs.

get(k)          = null
get(new Key(1)) = null
size            = 1

blocks.text:
`get(k)` looks in the bucket for id 2 (empty); `get(new Key(1))` finds the right bucket but the stored key now has id 2, so `equals` fails. The entry is stuck in the map forever. Fix: make key classes immutable (`final` fields, or a `record`).

### What changed in Java 8, and what to say in an interview

blocks.text: The last row deserves a line: `HashMap` is **not thread-safe**. In Java 7, two threads resizing at once could link two nodes into a cycle, after which `get` looped forever at 100 percent CPU. Java 8's tail-preserving resize removed that specific hang, but concurrent writers can still lose updates, corrupt the size or throw exceptions. If several threads write, use `ConcurrentHashMap` (next chapter), not `HashMap` and not a lock around `HashMap` unless you need compound operations across several keys.

blocks.title: Real world
blocks.text: Spring and most Java frameworks build request headers, JSON object fields, bean registries and caches on `HashMap`, `LinkedHashMap` or `ConcurrentHashMap`. When a service shows high CPU in `HashMap.get` or `HashMap$TreeNode.find` in a thread dump or profiler, the usual causes are a poor `hashCode` (all keys land in one bucket), a mutable key, or a map shared by several threads without synchronisation.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Explain how HashMap works internally. It is an array of buckets whose length is a power of two. `put` takes `key.hashCode()`, XORs its high 16 bits into the low 16, masks with `length - 1` to get the bucket, and walks the bucket comparing cached hashes and then `equals`. A new entry goes to the end of the chain. When the entry count exceeds capacity times load factor (default 16 and 0.75), the table doubles and entries are redistributed, each staying in its index or moving by the old length. A chain of 8 or more entries in a table of at least 64 buckets is converted to a red-black tree (and back at 6), making the worst case O(log n). Average `get` and `put` are O(1).

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: What happens if two different keys have the same hashCode? What if they are also equal? Same hash and not `equals`: they are stored in the same bucket as separate nodes (a collision), found by `equals`. Equal keys: the second `put` replaces the first one's value, because the map treats them as the same key.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- A HashMap is an array of buckets; the bucket is `(n - 1) & (h ^ (h >>> 16))`, entries in one bucket are found by cached hash and `equals`.
- The table is allocated on the first put, doubles when size exceeds capacity times 0.75, and splits each bucket in two on resize; presize with `HashMap.newHashMap(n)`.
- Long chains become red-black trees (threshold 8, table at least 64, back at 6), but only `Comparable` keys keep the O(log n) guarantee; a bad `hashCode` can still make a map hundreds of times slower.
- Keys must be immutable with consistent `equals` and `hashCode`; use `merge`, `computeIfAbsent` and `getOrDefault` instead of check-then-put.
- `HashMap` is not thread-safe, its iteration order is unspecified and its iterators are fail-fast.

sections.title: Choosing a data structure, and Big-O

blocks.text:
Most "which collection?" questions have a short answer once you know your access pattern: *how will I mostly read,* *insert, remove and iterate, and does order matter?* This chapter gives you the table, the reasoning behind it, and the cautions that stop you from over-optimising.

### Big-O in thirty seconds

**Big-O notation** describes how the cost of an operation grows with the number of elements n, ignoring constant factors. O(1) is constant, O(log n) grows very slowly (about 20 steps for a million elements), O(n) grows in proportion, and O(n log n) is the cost of a good sort. "Amortized O(1)" means that an occasional expensive operation (such as an array resize) is spread across many cheap ones. Big-O says nothing about the constant: an O(1) hash lookup may cost far more nanoseconds than an O(n) scan of a tiny array.

### The table

rows: amortized O(1) at end; O(n) middle
O(log n) worst case per bucket

blocks.text:
*Typical costs; n is the number of elements. Hash costs assume a well-distributed hashCode.*

### Memory overhead matters as much as speed

Every extra object costs a header (typically 12 bytes with compressed class pointers, rounded up to 8-byte alignment) plus a reference to it. A rough picture on a 64-bit HotSpot JVM with compressed references:

- `ArrayList<Integer>`: one 4-byte slot per element in the backing array, plus the `Integer` object itself (16 bytes) unless it is in the small cache. Primitives would be 4 bytes. This **boxing** overhead is why `int[]` or a primitive-specialised library wins on huge numeric data.
- `LinkedList`: a node per element (header + three references, about 24 bytes) on top of the element.
- `HashMap`: a node per entry (header + hash + key + value + next, about 32 bytes), plus the table array, which is kept at most 75 percent full by default.
- `HashSet` is a `HashMap` underneath, so it pays for the value slot too.
- `TreeMap`: a node per entry with key, value, left, right, parent and a colour flag, about 40 bytes.

These figures are estimates for a typical 64-bit JVM, not guarantees; measure with a tool such as JOL or a heap dump before relying on exact numbers.

### Does the complexity show up in practice?
