blocks.code:
$ java LookupCost.java
round 0: list 1836 ms, hash 2 ms, tree 21 ms
round 1: list 906 ms, hash 14 ms, tree 0 ms
round 2: list 680 ms, hash 8 ms, tree 0 ms
blocks.title: Typical output (measured on the build machine; will differ on yours)

blocks.text: Two thousand lookups in 100,000 elements cost hundreds of milliseconds in the list (each `contains` scans up to n elements) and a few milliseconds in the hash and tree sets. The exact numbers wobble because of JIT warm-up, which is also why you must never take one run as a benchmark.

blocks.title: Watch out
blocks.text: Micro-benchmarks written with `System.nanoTime()` in `main` mislead. The JIT compiler, garbage collector, and dead-code elimination all distort short loops. The program above is only good enough to show a difference of several orders of magnitude. For smaller differences use JMH (the Java Microbenchmark Harness) and compare on realistic data sizes.

### Decision guide

Ask the questions in order:

1. **Key-to-value lookup?** Use a `Map`. `HashMap` by default; `LinkedHashMap` if you need insertion or access order (or an LRU cache); `TreeMap` if you need sorted keys or range queries; `EnumMap` for enum keys; `ConcurrentHashMap` when threads share it.
2. **Uniqueness, no values?** Use a `Set`, with the same choices (`HashSet`, `LinkedHashSet`, `TreeSet`, `EnumSet`).
3. **Process in some order?** FIFO or LIFO: `ArrayDeque`. By priority: `PriorityQueue`. Between threads: a `BlockingQueue`.
4. **Otherwise a sequence?** `ArrayList`. Reach for `LinkedList` only if you have measured and know why.
5. **Read-only?** `List.of`, `Set.of`, `Map.of` and `copyOf` (see the chapter on immutable collections).

Declare variables by interface (`List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();`), so changing the implementation later is a one-line edit, and pass the narrowest interface a method needs.

#### Common interview picks

- Frequency count or "have I seen this?": `HashMap<K,Integer>` with `merge`, or `HashSet`.
- Two-sum, duplicates, anagram groups: `HashMap` / `HashSet` for O(1) lookups.
- Sorted order or "next greater key": `TreeMap`/`TreeSet` with `floorKey`/`ceilingKey`.
- Top-k, merge k sorted lists, running median: `PriorityQueue` (one or two).
- Breadth-first search: `ArrayDeque` as queue. Depth-first or undo history, matching brackets: `ArrayDeque` as stack.
- LRU cache: `LinkedHashMap` with access order, or a `HashMap` plus doubly linked list (built by hand in the next chapter).
- Sliding window maximum: a `Deque` holding indexes in decreasing value order.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: You have a million records to look up by id repeatedly. Which structure, and why? A `HashMap` from id to record: O(1) average lookup versus O(n) for scanning a list or O(log n) for a `TreeMap`. Pre-size it (`new HashMap<>(expected / 0.75f` `+ 1)` or `HashMap.newHashMap(expected)` in Java 19+) to avoid repeated resizing, and make sure the key class has a correct `equals` and a well-distributed `hashCode`. If you also need the records sorted by id, add a `TreeMap` or use it instead.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Choose by access pattern: lookup by key (`HashMap`), sorted (`TreeMap`), FIFO/LIFO (`ArrayDeque`), priority (`PriorityQueue`), sequence (`ArrayList`).
- Know the table: hash O(1) average, tree O(log n), array list O(1) index and O(n) search or middle insert, heap O(log n) offer/poll.
- Memory overhead (node objects, boxing, load factor) and cache locality often matter as much as the Big-O class.
- Declare by interface, trust the JDK defaults, and measure with a real benchmark harness before optimising.

sections.title: Implement your own: array list, linked list, hash map, LRU cache

blocks.text:
### LRU cache

Reading about data structures is not the same as building them. In this chapter you write four small ones from scratch: a dynamic array, a singly linked list, a hash map with chaining, and an LRU cache. Each is a few dozen lines, runs on its own, and checks itself. The goal is not to replace the JDK (never do that in production) but to make the earlier chapters concrete, and because "implement an LRU cache" is a classic interview task.

Each listing uses `assert` statements as tests. Assertions are **disabled by default**, so run with `java -ea File.java` (`-ea` means enable assertions); without the flag a failing check would pass silently. Printed output shows the state so you can follow along.

### A dynamic array

An `ArrayList` is an array that grows. The idea is a private `Object[]` plus a `size` counter: when the array is full, allocate a bigger one and copy. Doubling (rather than adding a fixed amount) makes `add` amortized O(1); the JDK grows by about 1.5 times, which trades a little time for less wasted space.

blocks.title: DynArray.java

blocks.code:
$ java -ea DynArray.java
caught: index 5, size 5
[ant, cat, dog, eel, fox] size=5
all DynArray checks passed
blocks.title: Run with assertions enabled

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- The array is `Object[]` and `get` casts to `E`. Generics are erased (see the chapter on generics), so you cannot write `new E[4]`; the unchecked cast is safe because only `add(E)` ever stores into the array.
- `remove` shifts the tail left with `System.arraycopy` (O(n)) and then nulls the vacated slot. Forgetting that last line is a classic memory leak: the array would keep a reference to an object the caller thinks is gone.
- Index checks throw `IndexOutOfBoundsException` with a useful message, as the real class does. Note the check is against `size`, not `items.length`.

### A singly linked list

A linked list stores each element in a **node** that points to the next node. There is no shifting and no resizing, but reaching the k-th element means following k links. Our list keeps only a `head` reference, so `addFirst` is O(1) and `addLast` walks the whole list, O(n). (`java.util.LinkedList` is doubly linked and keeps a `tail`, so both ends are O(1).)

blocks.title: SinglyLinkedList.java

blocks.code:
$ java -ea SinglyLinkedList.java
[1 -> 2 -> 3] size=3
reversed: [3 -> 2 -> 1]
after remove(2): [3 -> 1]
blocks.title: Run with assertions enabled

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `Node` is a `private static` nested class: it does not need the outer instance, so it does not carry the hidden reference an inner class would (see the chapter on nested classes).
- `remove` tracks a `prev` pointer so it can splice the node out; removing the head is a special case. These pointer cases are exactly where interview bugs happen: always test the head, the middle, the last node, and the empty list.
- `reverse` is the famous three-pointer loop: save `next`, point `cur.next` backwards, advance both. Draw it on paper once and it sticks. It runs in O(n) time and O(1) extra space.

### A hash map with chaining

Now the structure behind `HashMap` (see the chapter on HashMap in depth). The pieces are: a table of buckets, a way to turn a key into a bucket index, and a chain of entries per bucket to handle collisions (two keys landing in the same bucket).

blocks.title: MyHashMap.java

blocks.code:
$ java -ea MyHashMap.java
size=1003 capacity=2048
all MyHashMap checks passed
blocks.title: Run with assertions enabled

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- `hash` spreads the high bits into the low bits with `h ^ (h >>> 16)`, as the JDK does, because the index uses only the low bits.
- `hash & (length - 1)` equals `hash % length` when the length is a power of two, but is faster and never negative. This is why the table size doubles each time instead of growing by an arbitrary amount.
- When `size` exceeds 75 percent of the table length, `resize` doubles the table and **re-inserts every entry** (rehash), because the index depends on the table length. 1,003 entries ended at capacity 2048: 1,003 \> 768 (75 percent of 1024) forced the last doubling.
- A `null` key hashes to 0, like in the JDK. `Objects.equals` handles the null comparison.
- This version has no treeification, no `remove`, no iterators and is not thread-safe. Adding `remove` is a good exercise: it is the same `prev` splice as in the linked list.

blocks.title: Gotcha
blocks.text: If `hashCode` returns a constant, this map degrades to O(n) lookups. Every key lands in one bucket and the chain becomes a linked list. The JDK's `HashMap` softens the damage by converting long chains into red-black trees when the keys are `Comparable`, but a correct, well-spread `hashCode` is the real fix.

### An LRU cache

A **Least Recently Used (LRU) cache** holds at most `capacity` entries; when full, adding a new one evicts the entry that was used longest ago. Both `get` and `put` must be O(1). No single simple structure gives that, so we combine two:

- a `HashMap` from key to node, for O(1) lookup;
- a doubly linked list ordered by recency, with the most recently used at the front, for O(1) "move to front" and "remove the last".

Two **sentinel** nodes (`head` and `tail`, holding no data) remove all the null checks at the ends of the list.

blocks.title: LruCache.java

blocks.code:
$ java -ea LruCache.java
[c=3, a=1] (most recent first)
[d=4, a=10] (most recent first)
all LruCache checks passed
blocks.title: Run with assertions enabled

blocks.text:
#### What to notice

- Every successful `get` and `put` of an existing key calls `unlink` then `linkAfterHead`: that is the whole "recently used" mechanic.
- The eviction victim is always `tail.prev`, and its key is stored *in the node* so we can remove it from the index map too. That is why `Node` has a `key` field.
- Capacity 2: after `put a`, `put b`, `get a`, `put c`, the cache evicts `b` (not `a`), exactly as the printed state shows.

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.text: In real code you would not hand-write this. `LinkedHashMap` in access-order mode with `removeEldestEntry` is a three-line LRU cache (see the chapter on other maps), and Caffeine, a popular cache library that Spring Boot's cache support can use, adds thread safety, expiry and a better eviction policy. Writing it yourself once is for understanding and for interviews.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.text: Design an LRU cache with O(1) get and put. Combine a hash map (key to node) with a doubly linked list ordered by recency. On access, unlink the node and re-insert it at the front; on insert into a full cache, remove the node before the tail sentinel and delete its key from the map. Mention thread safety (wrap with a lock or use Caffeine) and that `LinkedHashMap(cap, 0.75f, true)` gives this for free.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
Key points

- Build structures from a few primitives: arrays that double (dynamic array), nodes with pointers (linked list), an array of chains indexed by a spread hash masked to a power of two (hash map).
- Resizing a hash table means rehashing every entry, since the index depends on the table length; the doubling policy keeps put at amortized O(1).
- An LRU cache is a hash map plus a doubly linked list with sentinels, giving O(1) get and put; `LinkedHashMap` in access order does the same in the JDK.
- Test with `assert` and run with `java -ea`; always cover the empty, single-element, first, middle and last cases.

#### Generics

items.question: What does this print, and why? `List<Integer> a = new ArrayList<>(); List<String> b = new ArrayList<>();` `System.out.println(a.getClass() == b.getClass());`
items.answer: `true`. After erasure both are the plain `ArrayList` class; type arguments exist only at compile time.

items.question: What is wrong with `List<Number> n = new ArrayList<Integer>();`, and how would you change the declaration so a method can read `Number`s from any list of numbers?
items.answer: Generics are invariant, so `List<Integer>` is not a `List<Number>`. Declare `List<? extends Number>` (or make the method generic) to read from any list of numbers.

items.question: Which wildcard do you choose for `copy(dest, src)` where `src` only gives you elements and `dest` only receives them? State the rule.
items.answer: `copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)`: PECS, Producer Extends (src), Consumer Super (dest).

items.question: Why does `new T[10]` not compile, and what is the usual workaround?
items.answer: The array's component type must be known at runtime but `T` is erased. Use a `List<T>`, or `(T[]) new Object[n]` with a private array, or `Array.newInstance(cls, n)` with a `Class<T>`.

items.question: In the `Erasure` listing, why does the `ClassCastException` happen at `strings.get(0)` and not at `raw.add(42)`?
items.answer: The raw `add` has no cast, so it succeeds and the list holds an `Integer`. The compiler inserted a `checkcast String` at the `get`, and that is where the mismatch is detected.

items.question: What is a bridge method and when does javac generate one?
items.answer: A synthetic method generated when erasure would break overriding, for example `compareTo(Object)` in a class implementing `Comparable<Animal>`, or a covariant return type. It casts and delegates to the real method.

blocks.text: #### The Collections Framework

items.question: Is `Map` a `Collection`? Name the three collection views a `Map` provides.
items.answer: No. `Map` is a separate hierarchy. Views: `keySet()`, `values()`, `entrySet()`.

items.question: What does this print? `List<String> l = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a","b","c")); for (String s : l) { if` `(s.equals("b")) l.remove(s); } System.out.println(l);`
items.answer: `[a, c]`. Removing the second-to-last element makes `hasNext()` return false, so the loop ends without a CME (verified by running).

items.question: Same code but the test is `s.equals("a")`. What happens and why?
items.answer: A `ConcurrentModificationException`: removing "a" changes `modCount`, and the next `next()` call detects it.

items.question: A class overrides `equals` but not `hashCode`. Which operation on a `HashSet` of that class fails, and which on an `ArrayList` still works?
items.answer: `contains`/`remove`/duplicate detection in the `HashSet` fail (wrong bucket); `ArrayList.contains` uses only `equals` and works.

items.question: Which of `ArrayList`, `LinkedList`, `ArrayDeque`, `PriorityQueue` implement `Deque`?
items.answer: `LinkedList` and `ArrayDeque`. `ArrayList` is only a `List`; `PriorityQueue` is a `Queue` but not a `Deque`.

items.question: What is wrong with `for (Integer i : list) list.add(i * 2);`?
items.answer: It modifies the list structurally during iteration, so the next iteration throws a CME. Build a separate result list or use a plain index loop.

blocks.text: #### Lists in depth

items.question: How many elements does `new ArrayList<>()` have room for right after construction, and after the first `add`? By what factor does it grow afterwards?
items.answer: Capacity 0 (lazy; the shared empty array), 10 after the first add, then roughly 1.5x (10, 15, 22, 33, ...) each time it fills.

items.question: What does this print? `List<Integer> l = new ArrayList<>(List.of(5, 6, 7, 1)); l.remove(1);` `System.out.println(l);` How do you remove the value 1 instead?
items.answer: `[5, 7, 1]` (index 1 removed). Use `l.remove(Integer.valueOf(1))`.

items.question: What happens with `List<String> l = Arrays.asList("a", "b"); l.set(0, "x"); l.add("c");`?
items.answer: `set` works and writes through to the array; `add` throws `UnsupportedOperationException` because the list has a fixed size.

items.question: Why is `for (int i = 0; i < list.size(); i++) list.get(i)` fast on `ArrayList` but a performance bug on `LinkedList`?
items.answer: `ArrayList.get` is an O(1) array read; `LinkedList.get(i)` walks nodes from an end, O(n), making the whole loop O(n squared). Use an iterator or for-each instead.

items.question: After `List<Integer> s = base.subList(1, 3); s.clear();` what happens to `base`? What if you then call `base.add(0)` and use `s` again?
items.answer: Elements 1 and 2 are removed from `base` too (it is a view). After `base.add(0)` the view is stale and using it throws `ConcurrentModificationException`.

items.question: Why prefer `ArrayDeque` over `Stack` and `LinkedList` for a stack?
items.answer: `Stack` is a legacy synchronized `Vector` subclass exposing list operations; `LinkedList` allocates a node per element. `ArrayDeque` is array-based, lighter and faster, and has the proper `push/pop/peek` API.

blocks.text: #### Sets

items.question: What data structure does `HashSet` use internally, and what is stored as the value?
items.answer: A `HashMap<E, Object>`; every entry maps the element to one shared dummy object (`PRESENT`).

items.question: What does this print? `Set<String> s = new TreeSet<>(Comparator.comparingInt(String::length));` `s.addAll(List.of("ab", "cd", "efg")); System.out.println(s);`
items.answer: `[ab, efg]`. "ab" and "cd" compare equal (same length), so "cd" is dropped.

items.question: You add a mutable object to a `HashSet`, change a field used by `hashCode`, then call `set.contains(obj)`. What is the likely result, and why?
items.answer: Most likely `false`. The object sits in the bucket for its old hash; `contains` now searches the bucket for the new hash.

items.question: Which set would you use for the days of the week on which a shop is open, and why?
items.answer: `EnumSet<DayOfWeek>`: a bit mask, so tiny, fast, type-safe and iterated in week order.

items.question: `TreeSet<Integer> t = new TreeSet<>(List.of(10, 20, 30)); t.ceiling(21)` and `t.lower(10)` return what?
items.answer: `30` and `null` (nothing is strictly lower than 10).

items.question: Why is `bigSet.removeAll(someList)` potentially slow, and what is the fix?
items.answer: For each element of `bigSet` it calls `someList.contains`, which is O(n), giving O(n times m). Pass a `HashSet` built from the list.

blocks.text: #### Other maps: LinkedHashMap, TreeMap and the specialists

items.question: How do you make a `LinkedHashMap` iterate in least-recently-used order, and how do you make it evict automatically?
items.answer: Use the constructor `new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true)` for access order; override `removeEldestEntry` to return `size() > capacity` for automatic eviction.

items.question: Given `TreeMap<Integer,String> m` with keys 10, 20, 30, what do `m.floorKey(25)`, `m.higherKey(30)` and `m.headMap(20).size()` return?
items.answer: `20`, `null` and `1` (headMap is exclusive of 20, so only key 10).

items.question: What is wrong with `if (!cmap.containsKey(k)) cmap.put(k, new ArrayList<>());` on a `ConcurrentHashMap`, and what replaces it?
items.answer: Another thread can insert between the check and the put (a race). Use `cmap.computeIfAbsent(k, x -> new` `ArrayList<>())`, which is atomic.

items.question: Why can a `WeakHashMap` entry fail to disappear even though the key is no longer used by your code?
items.answer: The value (or something else) still strongly references the key, or the key is a literal or cached object that is always strongly reachable.

items.question: Why does `new ConcurrentHashMap<String,String>().put("a", null)` throw?
items.answer: `ConcurrentHashMap` forbids null keys and values, since `get` returning null would be ambiguous in a concurrent setting.

items.question: What does `new IdentityHashMap<String,Integer>()` do with `put(new String("a"), 1); put(new String("a"),` `2);` and what is the size?
items.answer: It compares by reference, so the two `new String("a")` objects are different keys: size 2.

blocks.text: #### HashMap in depth

items.question: What are the default capacity and load factor of a `HashMap`, and when is the table created?
items.answer: 16 and 0.75. The table is allocated lazily on the first `put`.

items.question: `new HashMap<>(100)` followed by 100 puts: does the map resize? What about `HashMap.newHashMap(100)`?
items.answer: `new HashMap<>(100)` rounds to capacity 128 with threshold 96, so the 97th put resizes. `HashMap.newHashMap(100)` (Java 19+) gives a table of 256 and does not resize.

items.question: A key class overrides `equals` but not `hashCode`. What goes wrong with `map.put(new K(1), "a"); map.get(new` `K(1))`?
items.answer: The two keys have different identity-based hash codes, so they usually land in different buckets and `get` returns `null`, even though `equals` says they are the same.

items.question: What is wrong with this loop? `for (String k : map.keySet()) if (k.startsWith("tmp")) map.remove(k);` How do you fix it?
items.answer: Removing from the map while iterating its key set throws `ConcurrentModificationException`. Use `map.keySet().removeIf(k -> k.startsWith("tmp"))` or an explicit `Iterator.remove()`.

items.question: Why is the table length always a power of two? Give two reasons.
items.answer: Index computation is a fast mask `(n - 1) & hash` instead of a division, and resizing splits every bucket into exactly two destinations (same index or index plus old length) without rehashing.

items.question: What does this print? `Map<String,Integer> m = new HashMap<>(); m.put("a", null);` `System.out.println(m.getOrDefault("a", 9));`
items.answer: `null`: the key is present, so the default is not used.

blocks.text: #### Choosing a data structure, and Big-O

items.question: Which structure gives O(log n) `floorKey` and sorted iteration, and which gives O(1) average `get` but no order?
items.answer: `TreeMap` (or `TreeSet`); `HashMap` (or `HashSet`).

items.question: Why is `ArrayList.contains` O(n) even though `ArrayList.get(i)` is O(1)?
items.answer: `get(i)` indexes the array directly, but `contains` must compare the argument with elements one by one with `equals` until it finds a match.

items.question: What is the main memory disadvantage of `ArrayList<Integer>` compared with `int[]`?
items.answer: Boxing: each element is a separate `Integer` object (about 16 bytes) plus a reference in the array, against 4 bytes in the array of ints; poorer cache locality as well.

items.question: You need the 100 most recent events, discarding older ones automatically. Which collection do you build?
items.answer: A bounded `ArrayDeque` used as a ring: after each `addLast`, if `size() > 100` call `removeFirst`. (A `LinkedHashMap` with `removeEldestEntry` also works for keyed data.)

items.question: True or false: an O(1) algorithm is always faster than an O(n) one. Explain.
items.answer: False. Big-O hides constants and only describes growth; for small n a linear scan of a compact array can beat a hash lookup. Measure with realistic sizes.

blocks.text: #### Implement your own: array list, linked list, hash map, LRU cache

items.question: Run with assertions disabled, a failing `assert` does what? How do you enable them?
items.answer: Nothing: assertions are disabled by default and the statement is skipped. Enable with `java -ea` (`-enableassertions`).

items.question: Why must `DynArray.remove` set `items[size]` to `null` after shifting?
items.answer: Otherwise the array keeps a stale reference to the removed element past `size`, preventing garbage collection (a memory leak).

items.question: In `MyHashMap`, why is `hash & (length - 1)` a valid replacement for `hash % length`, and what requirement does that put on `length`?
items.answer: For a power-of-two `length`, the mask keeps exactly the low bits, which equals the remainder, and it is never negative. So the table length must always be a power of two.

items.question: What is wrong with this `reverse`? `cur.next = prev; prev = cur; cur = cur.next;`
items.answer: After `cur.next = prev`, `cur.next` points backwards, so `cur = cur.next` moves back to the previous node (or null): the rest of the list is lost. Save `next` first.

items.question: Why does the LRU cache keep the key inside each node as well as in the map?
items.answer: When evicting `tail.prev`, you only have the node; you need its key to delete the matching entry from the index map.

items.question: What is the time complexity of `SinglyLinkedList.addLast` here, and how would you make it O(1)?
items.answer: O(n), because it walks to the end. Keep a `tail` reference and update it on insert and remove to get O(1).
